title: Research Methods in SLT
source_note: Grounded in standard research-methodology content for science/medical laboratory technology programmes: research design, sampling, data collection instruments, variables, hypothesis testing, basic biostatistics, ethics, and scientific report/thesis writing, as taught at the 300 level.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a literature review in a research study?
options: To pad the length of the final report
To identify existing knowledge, gaps, and context for the current study
To replace the need for data collection
To list the researcher's personal opinions
questions.correct_answer: To identify existing knowledge, gaps, and context for the current study
questions.explanation: A literature review situates the study within existing knowledge and reveals gaps the research aims to address.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a research hypothesis?
options: A proven scientific fact
A tentative, testable statement about the relationship between variables
A summary of prior research findings
The final conclusion of a study
questions.correct_answer: A tentative, testable statement about the relationship between variables
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction about a relationship between variables, not an established fact.

questions.question: In an experiment testing a new reagent's effect on assay sensitivity, what is the independent variable?
options: The assay sensitivity result
The type/concentration of reagent used
The laboratory temperature
The technician's experience level
questions.correct_answer: The type/concentration of reagent used
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the factor manipulated by the researcher; here it is the reagent used.

questions.question: What distinguishes a dependent variable from an independent variable?
options: The dependent variable is manipulated; the independent is measured
The dependent variable is the measured outcome that responds to the independent variable
They are always the same variable
The dependent variable is chosen randomly
questions.correct_answer: The dependent variable is the measured outcome that responds to the independent variable
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome measured, expected to change in response to manipulation of the independent variable.

questions.question: Which sampling technique gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection?
options: Convenience sampling
Purposive sampling
Simple random sampling
Snowball sampling
questions.correct_answer: Simple random sampling
questions.explanation: Simple random sampling ensures every population member has an equal and independent chance of being selected.

questions.question: A researcher divides a population of hospital patients into strata by department, then randomly samples from each stratum. This is an example of which sampling method?
options: Cluster sampling
Stratified random sampling
Quota sampling
Systematic sampling
questions.correct_answer: Stratified random sampling
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into homogeneous subgroups (strata) and randomly samples within each.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-probability sampling technique?
options: Simple random sampling
Systematic sampling
Convenience sampling
Stratified sampling
questions.correct_answer: Convenience sampling
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling selects readily available subjects and does not give every unit a known probability of selection.

questions.question: What is the main difference between qualitative and quantitative research?
options: Qualitative research uses numbers; quantitative uses words
Qualitative research explores meanings/experiences; quantitative measures and quantifies variables numerically
There is no real difference
Quantitative research cannot be statistically analyzed
questions.correct_answer: Qualitative research explores meanings/experiences; quantitative measures and quantifies variables numerically
questions.explanation: Qualitative research is concerned with non-numerical meaning and experience, while quantitative research relies on numerical measurement and statistical analysis.

questions.question: Which research design would be most appropriate to determine the prevalence of malaria parasitaemia in a community at a single point in time?
options: Cross-sectional study
Longitudinal cohort study
Case-control study
Randomized controlled trial
questions.correct_answer: Cross-sectional study
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional study measures the prevalence of a condition in a population at one point in time.

questions.question: In a case-control study, participants are selected based on:
options: Their exposure status
Their outcome/disease status
Random allocation to treatment groups
Their age only
questions.correct_answer: Their outcome/disease status
questions.explanation: Case-control studies select subjects based on whether they already have the outcome (cases) or not (controls), then look backward for exposures.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of a randomized controlled trial (RCT)?
options: Subjects choose which group to join
Subjects are randomly assigned to intervention or control groups
It only uses secondary data
It has no control group
questions.correct_answer: Subjects are randomly assigned to intervention or control groups
questions.explanation: Random allocation to intervention and control groups is the hallmark of an RCT, minimizing selection bias.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary data collection instrument commonly used in laboratory-based clinical research?
options: A structured laboratory results proforma/data sheet
A published textbook
A newspaper article
A movie review
questions.correct_answer: A structured laboratory results proforma/data sheet
questions.explanation: Primary data in laboratory research is often collected using structured data sheets or proformas designed for the study.

questions.question: What does 'validity' of a research instrument refer to?
options: Whether the instrument measures what it is intended to measure
Whether the instrument gives the same result every time
The cost of the instrument
How quickly the instrument can be used
questions.correct_answer: Whether the instrument measures what it is intended to measure
questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether an instrument accurately measures the construct it claims to measure.

questions.question: What does 'reliability' of a research instrument refer to?
options: The consistency/repeatability of results obtained using the instrument
The accuracy of the instrument compared to a gold standard
The price of the instrument
Whether the instrument is approved by an ethics committee
questions.correct_answer: The consistency/repeatability of results obtained using the instrument
questions.explanation: Reliability refers to the consistency of measurements obtained on repeated use under the same conditions.

questions.question: In statistics, what is a 'population' in the research context?
options: The entire set of individuals or items of interest to the researcher
Only the people who respond to a survey
The number of pages in a research report
The statistical software used
questions.correct_answer: The entire set of individuals or items of interest to the researcher
questions.explanation: A population is the complete set of elements the researcher wants to study or draw conclusions about.

questions.question: A 'sample' in research is best described as:
options: A subset of the population selected for study
A duplicate of the entire population
A type of laboratory reagent
The research hypothesis
questions.correct_answer: A subset of the population selected for study
questions.explanation: A sample is a smaller, manageable subset drawn from the larger population for study.

questions.question: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme outlier values?
options: Mode
Median
Mean
Range
questions.correct_answer: Mean
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean incorporates every value, so extreme outliers pull it disproportionately compared to the median or mode.

questions.question: What is a p-value used for in hypothesis testing?
options: To measure the probability that the observed results (or more extreme) occurred by chance, assuming the null hypothesis is true
To calculate the sample size directly
To measure the cost of the study
To determine the population mean exactly
questions.correct_answer: To measure the probability that the observed results (or more extreme) occurred by chance, assuming the null hypothesis is true
questions.explanation: The p-value estimates the probability of obtaining results as extreme as observed under the null hypothesis.

questions.question: If a p-value of 0.03 is obtained and the significance level (alpha) is set at 0.05, what is the correct conclusion?
options: Reject the null hypothesis; the result is statistically significant
Accept the null hypothesis; the result is not significant
The study must be repeated before any conclusion
The p-value has no relation to significance
questions.correct_answer: Reject the null hypothesis; the result is statistically significant
questions.explanation: Since 0.03 is less than the alpha of 0.05, the null hypothesis is rejected, indicating statistical significance.

questions.question: What is the null hypothesis (H0) in a research study?
options: A statement asserting no effect or no difference between groups
A statement guaranteed to be true
The researcher's preferred outcome
A statement only used in qualitative research
questions.correct_answer: A statement asserting no effect or no difference between groups
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis proposes that there is no significant effect or relationship, which the study tests against.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a Type I error?
options: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive)
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative)
Correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
Correctly accepting a true null hypothesis
questions.correct_answer: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive)
questions.explanation: A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected, i.e., a false positive result.

questions.question: Which statistical test is most appropriate to compare the means of two independent groups with normally distributed data?
options: Chi-square test
Student's t-test
Pearson correlation
Kruskal-Wallis test
questions.correct_answer: Student's t-test
questions.explanation: The independent-samples t-test compares means of two independent groups when data are approximately normally distributed.

questions.question: Which statistical test is appropriate for examining the association between two categorical variables?
options: Chi-square test
Paired t-test
ANOVA
Linear regression
questions.correct_answer: Chi-square test
questions.explanation: The chi-square test of independence assesses whether there is an association between two categorical variables.

questions.question: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) is primarily used to:
options: Compare means across three or more groups
Compare two proportions
Determine sample size
Test correlation between two continuous variables only
questions.correct_answer: Compare means across three or more groups
questions.explanation: ANOVA tests whether there are statistically significant differences among the means of three or more independent groups.

questions.question: In research ethics, what does 'informed consent' mean?
options: Participants agree to take part after being fully informed of the study's purpose, risks, and benefits
The researcher decides on behalf of participants
Consent obtained after the study has been completed
A form signed only by the research supervisor
questions.correct_answer: Participants agree to take part after being fully informed of the study's purpose, risks, and benefits
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that participants understand and voluntarily agree to participate based on full disclosure of relevant study information.

questions.question: Why is confidentiality important when handling patient laboratory data in research?
options: It protects participants' privacy and builds trust in the research process
It is not important in laboratory research
It allows researchers to publish patient names freely
It has no bearing on ethics approval
questions.correct_answer: It protects participants' privacy and builds trust in the research process
questions.explanation: Confidentiality safeguards participant privacy, an essential ethical obligation in research involving human data or samples.

questions.question: What is the role of an Institutional Research Ethics Committee (REC/IRB)?
options: To review and approve research protocols to ensure ethical standards are met
To fund research projects
To publish research articles
To manage laboratory equipment procurement
questions.correct_answer: To review and approve research protocols to ensure ethical standards are met
questions.explanation: Ethics committees review proposed research to protect participant welfare and ensure ethical compliance before approval.

questions.question: Which section of a standard research report presents the interpretation and significance of findings?
options: Abstract
Methodology
Discussion
References
questions.correct_answer: Discussion
questions.explanation: The discussion section interprets results, compares them with existing literature, and explains their significance.

questions.question: What should the 'Methodology' section of a research report describe?
options: The background literature only
How the study was conducted, including design, sampling, materials, and procedures
The researcher's personal biography
Only the final conclusions
questions.correct_answer: How the study was conducted, including design, sampling, materials, and procedures
questions.explanation: The methodology section details the study design, sample, materials, and procedures used, enabling replication.

questions.question: In referencing a scientific work, what is the primary purpose of citations?
options: To acknowledge original sources and avoid plagiarism
To increase the word count of the report
To confuse the reader
Citations are optional and unnecessary in science
questions.correct_answer: To acknowledge original sources and avoid plagiarism
questions.explanation: Citations give credit to original authors and allow readers to trace the sources of information, preventing plagiarism.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines 'plagiarism' in academic research?
options: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as one's own without proper attribution
Citing a source correctly
Using your own previous data
Collaborating with a co-author with permission
questions.correct_answer: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as one's own without proper attribution
questions.explanation: Plagiarism is the act of using another's work or ideas without giving proper credit, considered a serious academic offense.

questions.question: A pilot study is conducted primarily to:
options: Test and refine the research instruments and procedures on a small scale before the main study
Replace the need for a full-scale study
Publish preliminary results as final findings
Determine the study's ethical approval status
questions.correct_answer: Test and refine the research instruments and procedures on a small scale before the main study
questions.explanation: A pilot study is a small-scale trial run to identify and correct issues with instruments or procedures before the full study.

questions.question: What is meant by 'bias' in research?
options: Any systematic error that distorts the true relationship between variables
A random error that occurs equally in all directions
A statistical test used to compare groups
The final approved research report
questions.correct_answer: Any systematic error that distorts the true relationship between variables
questions.explanation: Bias is a systematic (non-random) error that skews results away from the true value, affecting validity.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of selection bias?
options: Choosing only hospital patients with severe disease to represent the general population
Randomly selecting equal numbers from each subgroup
Using a validated questionnaire
Applying a standardized laboratory protocol
questions.correct_answer: Choosing only hospital patients with severe disease to represent the general population
questions.explanation: Selection bias arises when the sample is not representative of the population, such as selecting only severe cases.

questions.question: In laboratory-based research, what does 'quality control' primarily ensure?
options: That test results are accurate, precise, and reliable
That the study is completed faster
That participants are recruited more easily
That the report has no grammatical errors
questions.correct_answer: That test results are accurate, precise, and reliable
questions.explanation: Quality control procedures monitor and verify that laboratory test results meet accuracy and precision standards.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using a control group in an experimental study?
options: To provide a baseline for comparison against the group receiving the intervention
To increase the sample size artificially
To eliminate the need for statistical analysis
To reduce the cost of the study only
questions.correct_answer: To provide a baseline for comparison against the group receiving the intervention
questions.explanation: A control group serves as a baseline, allowing researchers to isolate the effect of the intervention being studied.

questions.question: A confidence interval of 95% around a mean value means:
options: We are 95% confident the true population parameter lies within that interval
95% of the sample data falls exactly on the mean
There is a 95% chance the study is error-free
The result is significant at all times
questions.correct_answer: We are 95% confident the true population parameter lies within that interval
questions.explanation: A 95% confidence interval indicates that if the study were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true population parameter.
